procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated March 25, 1965, of the Railway Rates Tribunal, Madras in Complaint No. 3 of 1963, determining reasonable rates for siding charges.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. (P) Ltd. filed a complaint before the Railway Rates Tribunal, Madras. The Tribunal determined that the existing charges being recovered by the North Eastern Railway were unreasonable and unjustified. The North Eastern Railway appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the Tribunal's order.

directions: the appeal fails and is dismissed with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the rule that no evidence can be looked into upon a plea which was never put forward applies to a case where parties go to trial with knowledge that a particular question is in issue, though no specific issue has been framed thereon, and adduce evidence relating thereto.

facts: The parties went to trial with the knowledge that a particular question was in issue, even though no specific issue had been formally framed on that point.
Both parties adduced evidence relating to this question.
The lower Tribunal found as a matter of fact that the Railway was ready with the required evidence and that no prejudice had been caused to it by the lack of a specific framed issue.
law: The general rule, as stated by the Privy Council, is that "no amount of evidence can be looked into upon a plea which was never put forward."
However, the Supreme Court, citing its own precedent in *Nagubai Ammal v. B. Shama Rao*, clarified the scope of this rule.
The rule's purpose is to prevent a decision from being based on an issue that was not present in the minds of the parties and on which they had no opportunity to present evidence.
This rule does not apply to cases where parties knowingly go to trial on a particular question and adduce evidence on it, despite the absence of a formally framed issue.
application: The Court applied the exception to the general rule. It reasoned that since the parties knew the question was at issue and presented evidence, the purpose of the rule (to prevent surprise and prejudice) was not violated.
The Court deferred to the Tribunal's finding of fact that the Railway was prepared with its evidence and suffered no prejudice.
Therefore, the absence of a formally framed issue was not a valid reason to disregard the evidence that the parties had knowingly presented.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the rule against looking at evidence for an unpleaded issue does not apply when parties are aware that a question is in issue, go to trial on it, and present evidence, especially when no prejudice is caused to either party.

issue.issue_text: Whether the charges for carriage of goods to points or places not forming part of the railway are covered by the expression 'any other charge' under s. 41(1)(c) of the Indian Railways Act, thereby making the complaint competently entertained by the Tribunal.

facts: The case involved a dispute over charges levied by the railway for the carriage of goods.
Specifically, the issue concerned charges for carrying goods to points or places that were not part of the railway's own network.
A complaint regarding the reasonableness of these charges was filed with the Railway Rates Tribunal.
law: The relevant law is Section 41(1)(c) of the Indian Railways Act, which allows a complaint to be made to the Tribunal regarding "any other charge which is unreasonable."
The Court also considered Section 29(2) of the Act, which it correlated with Section 41(1)(c), as both sections use the expression "any other charge."
application: The Supreme Court rejected a narrow interpretation of the expression "any other charge" as used in Sections 29(2) and 41(1)(c).
The Court reasoned that this expression should not be limited only to charges related to the core statutory duties of the railway.
It held that the phrase was intended to cover charges levied by the railway for "all other services" it provides.

Applying this broad interpretation, the Court explicitly stated that charges for the carriage of goods from the railway to points or places not forming part of the railway are "certainly" covered by the expression "any other charge" under Section 41(1)(c).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the charges for carrying goods to places not forming part of the railway were covered by the expression 'any other charge' in Section 41(1)(c). Therefore, the complaint was competently filed, and the Tribunal had the jurisdiction to entertain it.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, not sitting as a regular court of appeal from the Tribunal's decisions, should interfere with a pure finding of fact made by the Tribunal.

facts: The Railway Rates Tribunal made a conclusion that was a "pure finding of fact".
The appellant challenged this finding of fact in their appeal to the Supreme Court.
law: The Supreme Court does not sit as a regular court of appeal from the decisions of the Tribunal.
As a result, the Supreme Court does not ordinarily interfere with or go into questions of fact decided by the Tribunal.
application: The Court noted that the Tribunal had based its finding on "ample evidence" from which it could have reasonably reached its conclusion.
The appellant failed to show any reason why this "pure finding of fact" should be displaced or overturned.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided not to interfere with the Tribunal's finding of fact, holding that it is not its role to act as a regular court of appeal on such matters, especially when the finding was based on reasonable evidence and no reason was shown to displace it.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the rule that no evidence can be looked into upon a plea which was never put forward applies to a case where parties go to trial with knowledge that a particular question is in issue, though no specific issue has been framed thereon, and adduce evidence relating thereto.
appellant_arguments: The Tribunal was not justified in adjudicating upon the charges for the maintenance of the assisted siding because the issue was not explicitly raised in the pleadings.
Citing the Privy Council, the appellant argued that 'no amount of evidence can be looked into upon a plea which was never put forward.'
respondent_arguments: The appellant (the Railway) was not misled or surprised by the issue being raised, as they were fully aware that the maintenance charges had to be justified.
The appellant was ready with the required evidence on the matter before the trial began, and therefore no prejudice was caused to them.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the charges for carriage of goods to points or places not forming part of the railway are covered by the expression 'any other charge' under s. 41(1)(c) of the Indian Railways Act, thereby making the complaint competently entertained by the Tribunal.
appellant_arguments: The Tribunal lacked jurisdiction under s. 41(1)(c) of the Act to determine the reasonableness of charges for maintaining the assisted siding.
respondent_arguments: The charges for the assisted siding fall under the scope of s. 41(1)(c) of the Act, giving the Tribunal the jurisdiction to hear the complaint.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, not sitting as a regular court of appeal from the Tribunal's decisions, should interfere with a pure finding of fact made by the Tribunal.
appellant_arguments: The Tribunal erred in its finding of fact that the Railway was not entitled to haulage charges for lines 3 and 4.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court should not interfere with the Tribunal's decision as it is a pure finding of fact and the Court is not sitting as a regular court of appeal.
The appellant has not shown that the Tribunal misdirected itself or provided any reason to displace its finding of fact.

cases.case_name: Rani Chandra Kunwar v. Chaudhri Narpat Singh
cases.principle: Evidence can be considered on a question that parties knew was in issue and on which they adduced evidence, even if no specific issue was framed thereon.

cases.case_name: Nagubai Ammal v. B. Shama Rao
cases.principle: The rule that evidence on an issue not raised in pleadings should be disregarded has no application where parties go to trial with knowledge that a particular question is in issue and adduce evidence relating thereto.

cases.case_name: Union of India v. The Indian Sugar Mills Association
cases.principle: A complaint to the Tribunal was competent under s. 41(1)(c) of the Indian Railways Act, 1890.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Evidence presented on issues that parties knowingly contested during a trial can form the basis of a decision on that issue, even if it was not formally framed. This principle does not apply to a different issue that was not in the minds of the parties and on which they had no opportunity to present evidence.
obiter: The Supreme Court does not function as a regular court of appeal from tribunal decisions and, in such cases, does not ordinarily review questions of fact.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appeal was dismissed because the Court found no reason to interfere with the Tribunal's decision. The Court held that the rule against considering unpleaded issues does not apply when parties are aware of the issue and present evidence without prejudice. It also affirmed the Tribunal's jurisdiction by broadly interpreting the phrase "any other charge" in the Indian Railways Act. Finally, the Court refused to overturn the Tribunal's findings of fact, emphasizing its limited appellate role and the presence of ample evidence supporting the Tribunal's conclusion.
legal_tests_applied: The rule that no evidence can be looked into upon a plea which was never put forward has no application to a case where parties go to trial with knowledge that a particular question is in issue, though no specific issue has been framed thereon, and when evidence relating thereto had been adduced.

The expression 'any other charge' under s. 29(2) and s. 41(1)(c) of the Indian Railways Act cannot be given a narrow meaning so as to exclude charges made or levied by the Railway for all other services beyond its core statutory duty.

The Supreme Court, not sitting as a regular court of appeal from a Tribunal's decision, does not ordinarily go into questions of fact and will not displace a pure finding of fact unless a specific reason is shown to do so.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the Tribunal wrongly considered an unpleaded issue failed because the Tribunal found that the appellant was ready with the required evidence and no prejudice had been caused to it.

The appellant's challenge to the Tribunal's jurisdiction was rejected because the Court held that the expression 'any other charge' under the Indian Railways Act was broad enough to cover the disputed siding charges.

The appellant's request to overturn the Tribunal's factual finding was denied because no reason was shown for displacing the finding, which was supported by ample evidence, and the Supreme Court does not act as a regular court of appeal on facts from the Tribunal.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that the procedural rule regarding pleadings should not apply because the appellant was aware of the issue concerning maintenance charges, was prepared with evidence, and therefore suffered no prejudice.

The respondent's position that the Tribunal had jurisdiction was upheld, as the Court agreed that the siding charges fell within the scope of 'any other charge' under s. 41(1)(c) of the Indian Railways Act.

The respondent prevailed by arguing that the Supreme Court should not interfere with the Tribunal's decision, as it was a pure finding of fact supported by evidence, and the Court's appellate role in such cases is limited.
policy_considerations: Judicial deference to specialized tribunals: The Court emphasized that it does not sit as a regular court of appeal from the Tribunal's decisions and, therefore, will not ordinarily interfere with its findings of fact, respecting the expertise and role of the specialized body.

Substance over procedural technicality: The Court endorsed the principle that a case should not fail on a technical pleading defect if both parties were fully aware of the issue at trial, presented evidence on it, and no prejudice was caused.
